PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6654 – Reuters estimate
body: The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets.

China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours.

Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations.

Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.

In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

news.title: USDCAD bounces off the 100 hour MA. Buyers remain in control.
body: USDCAD is taking a breather after its steady climb from the early-November low at 1.3929. The pair has traded in a 44-pip range today, below the roughly 63-pip average over the past month. The narrower range suggests consolidation as traders weigh the next move.

The low today reached 1.4274, just above the rising 100 hour moving average (blue line on the chart above), currently at 1.4271. That area also corresponds with the highs from last Thursday and Friday and provided a base yesterday before buyers pushed higher (see red numbered circles). .

That makes it a key downside barometer and increases it's importance going forward. Stay above, and buyers retain control. Move below, and sellers would have an opening for a deeper correction. Over the next day, watch that level for your trading clues and short term bias.

Earlier today, buyers extended above the swing highs from the first half of October between 1.42918 and 1.42986. That is close restance that if broken would have traders thinking there is more room to roam to the upside. Today, the break took the price to 1.43154—the highest level since April 2025—but momentum stalled.
The immediate challenge for buyers is to reclaim and hold above 1.42918–1.42986. Doing so would put today’s high at 1.43154 back in play.
A break above that high would open the door for further upside, with the daily chart highlighting the March and April 2025 swing highs between 1.4397 and 1.4413 as a broader target.
For now, the rising 100 hour moving average defines support, while 1.42918–1.42986 is the hurdle buyers need to clear to get the upside moving again.

news.title: Fed's Williams: The economy is getting stronger, inflation not moving in the right direction
body: New York Fed President John Williams is out with some fresh commentary, and the message is a classic mix of acknowledging the inflation headache while trying to keep the market from pricing in anything too aggressive.

The big takeaway here for traders is that line about avoiding "dramatic policy action." Coming off the back of this week's hot October CPI print—and with the market increasingly jittery about the Fed having to ramp up its hiking cycle after restarting it in September—Williams is effectively pouring cold water on the idea of a 50 bps move.

Still, you can't ignore the hawkish undertones. Admitting that tariff and energy shocks are spilling over into the broader data is a notable shift. Back in October, Williams was singing a much more patient tune, arguing there was "no need for urgency" ahead of the late-October FOMC meeting and suggesting he saw no need for hikes in 2027. While he was open to one more quarter-point hike before year-end back then, the tone today is noticeably more concerned about the stickiness of prices—even if he isn't ready to panic.
For the December 9 decision, a 25 bps hike remains the clear base case and it's fully priced into markets with a dwindling chance of 50 bps.
